Its process-global cache PRICE_MAP_CACHE (static HashMap<String, CacheEntry>, price_map.rs:32-38) is keyed on `format!("{}:{}:{}:{}", mode, time_window, property_type, city)` at :125-131, where `city` (:53) and `property_type` (:55) are free-form, unvalidated user strings echoed straight into the key.

frontend/apps/mobile/src/hooks/useApi.ts:82-91 — the central `apiRequest` helper (backing every useQuery/useMutation in the app) reads the bearer token from SecureStore once (:66) and, on any non-ok response, just `throw new Error(message)` (:91). There is NO 401 branch, NO token-refresh attempt, and NO single-retry after refresh. A 401 from an expired access token is surfaced to the UI as a generic error identical to any other HTTP failure.

The recovery capability EXISTS but is never wired in: contexts/AuthContext.tsx defines `refreshToken()` (:209) that reads `ppt_refresh_token` from SecureStore and POSTs `/api/v1/auth/refresh` (:217-222). Grep across the whole app confirms `refreshToken()` is invoked ONLY from tests (test/integration/auth.integration.test.tsx:405,433,460) — never from production code. There is no `setInterval`/`setTimeout` proactive refresh and no 401 interceptor in AuthContext or useApi.

Impact: the backend uses short-lived access tokens with refresh-token rotation (docs/api/README.md). Once the access-token TTL lapses — which is guaranteed to happen in any normal session — every authenticated query and mutation fails with a spurious error, even though the client holds a valid refresh token that would transparently restore the session. The user is effectively soft-logged-out until they manually kill and re-login. Fix: in `apiRequest`, on a 401, call `AuthContext.refreshToken()` (or a shared refresh routine) once and retry the request; or add a proactive refresh timer keyed off the access-token `exp` claim (the code already decodes JWT claims via utils/jwt in getTenantId). Confidence medium: the missing-wiring is unambiguous from source; exact TTL-triggered timing is not runtime-confirmed.

frontend/apps/mobile/src/nfc/NFCAccessController.ts:249-346 — `validateAccess` decides credential expiry (`new Date(credential.validUntil) < now`, :275) and time-of-day access windows (:299-336) entirely from device-local `new Date()` (:250, `now.getHours()`/`now.getDay()` :301-303). Device wall-clock is user-controllable; a holder of an expired or time-restricted credential can roll the phone clock back to make `validateAccess` return `granted: true`.

That client-side `granted` result is not merely advisory display: it GATES the physical transmit — `NativeNFC.transmitCredential(credential.encryptedData)` is only reached when `validationResult.granted` (NFCAccessController.ts:190-196). So clock tampering directly changes whether the credential is presented to the reader.

Impact: if the door reader / backend does NOT independently re-validate expiry and time-restrictions server-side, this is a physical-access bypass; if it does, this is still a defense-in-depth gap that lets revoked/expired credentials be transmitted. Fix: derive `now` from a trusted/monotonic or server-synced time source for the expiry + time-restriction checks (or make the reader authoritative and treat the client gate as UX-only). Confidence medium: exploitability depends on reader-side enforcement which is out of this segment's scope, but relying solely on device clock for credential expiry is a confirmed anti-pattern in the source.

When a stored condition JSON deserializes as neither ConditionGroup nor Condition, the `else` branch (lines 481-486) only logs `tracing::warn!("Could not parse condition, skipping")` and continues; it does NOT return Ok(false). If every condition in the list is unparseable (or the malformed one is the only gating predicate), the loop falls through to `Ok(true)` at line 489.

This directly gates side-effecting action execution: the sole caller (workflow_executor.rs:344 `if !self.evaluate_conditions(&conditions, &context)? { ... continue; }`) skips the workflow only when the gate returns false. A malformed/schema-drifted condition therefore causes the workflow's actions (email/notification/api_call — services/actions/*) to fire UNCONDITIONALLY on every matching trigger event, instead of being blocked.

Reachable in production via execute/process workflow-event path; conditions are author-supplied JSON persisted on the workflow row (`workflow.conditions.0`), so a new operator, a removed field, or any serde-shape drift silently flips a gated automation into an always-on one. A gate should fail CLOSED on uninterpretable input — return Ok(false) (or propagate a WorkflowError) when a condition cannot be parsed, rather than skipping it. Note evaluate_single_condition errors already propagate via `?` (fail-closed); only the serde parse path fails open.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/workflow_executor.rs:527-538 — evaluate_condition_group() for LogicalOperator::Not silently evaluates only ONE child. It negates `group.conditions.first()` and, when that Some-branch is taken, entirely ignores every remaining entry in `group.conditions` AND all of `group.groups`. The code comment at line 528 even states 'only first condition is considered'.

Unlike And/Or (lines 499-526) which fold over BOTH `conditions` and nested `groups`, the Not arm has no fold. A workflow author expressing NOT over multiple predicates (e.g. intending NOT(A AND B), or a NOT wrapping a nested group while also carrying a stray condition) gets NOT(A) — a silently-wrong gate result with no error surfaced.

Same gating path as the fail-open finding (feeds workflow_executor.rs:344 action-execution decision), so an incorrectly-negated group can either run actions that should be blocked or block actions that should run. Fix: evaluate the Not group's full child set (negate the AND/OR fold of all conditions + nested groups), or reject a Not group carrying more than one child at validation time so the ambiguity cannot be persisted.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/workflow_executor.rs:610-621 — the ComparisonOperator::Matches arm calls `regex::Regex::new(pattern)` (line 618) on every single condition evaluation. Regex compilation is the expensive step in the `regex` crate; recompiling it per evaluate_single_condition call, inside the per-event × per-condition workflow-evaluation loop, wastes CPU proportional to (triggered workflows × conditions) for each inbound trigger event.

The compiled Regex depends only on the author-supplied `pattern` string stored on the condition, so it is a natural candidate for a compile-once cache (e.g. a keyed cache on the executor, or precompiling condition regexes when the workflow is loaded). No correctness impact — efficiency/DX only. (The Rust `regex` crate is backtracking-free, so this is not a ReDoS concern, only a redundant-compilation cost.)

backend/servers/api-server/src/routes/voice_webhooks.rs:948-960 — verify_hmac_signature() FAILS OPEN: line 950 `std::env::var("VOICE_WEBHOOK_SECRET").unwrap_or_else(|_| "default_secret".to_string())`. When the env var is unset, the receiver validates inbound webhook signatures against the hardcoded, source-visible constant "default_secret", so any attacker can forge a valid HMAC-SHA256 signature and pass verification.

Reachable in production: the router is mounted at `/api/v1/webhooks/voice` (backend/servers/api-server/src/lib.rs:339-340 via voice_webhook_router()), exposing POST /verify -> verify_webhook_signature -> verify_hmac_signature (voice_webhooks.rs:71, 712, 948). Inconsistent with the fail-closed pattern used by every sibling receiver: DocuSign/Adobe/HelloSign in integrations/webhook.rs:778/808/837 return 500 CONFIG_ERROR when their secret env var is empty, and PORTAL/AIRBNB/STRIPE secrets fail closed per backend/CLAUDE.md. backend/servers/api-server/src/routes/voice_webhooks.rs:959 — webhook signature is verified with a non-constant-time comparison: `Ok(signature == expected)`, where `expected` is the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of the body. String `==` short-circuits on the first differing byte, exposing a timing side-channel that can be used to recover a valid signature byte-by-byte.

The codebase already knows the correct pattern and applies it elsewhere in the same segment: signatures.rs:679 uses `subtle::ct_eq` under a length guard, and caddy_ask.rs:181 uses a length-checked constant-time compare. voice_webhooks.rs is the lone signature-verification path using raw `==`.

Reachable via the mounted POST /api/v1/webhooks/voice/verify path (lib.rs:339-340 -> voice_webhooks.rs:71 -> 712 -> 959). Fix: compare with a constant-time primitive (subtle::ConstantTimeEq / ct_eq) after a length check, matching signatures.rs.

backend/servers/api-server/src/routes/voice_webhooks.rs:963-999 — authenticate_voice_user() performs NO token validation: the `_access_token` parameter is unused (underscore-prefixed) and the function returns whatever device the query `SELECT * FROM voice_assistant_devices WHERE platform = $1 AND is_active = TRUE ORDER BY last_used_at DESC NULLS LAST LIMIT 1` returns — i.e. an arbitrary active device for the platform, not the device/user bound to the presented token. backend/servers/reality-server/src/state.rs:698-712 — TokenValidationCache::set(), when the cache is full after expired-entry eviction, claims to 'remove oldest entries' (inline comment) but actually removes ARBITRARY entries. It builds keys_to_remove from `cache.iter().take(entries_to_remove)` over a std HashMap, whose iteration order is unspecified/randomized. There is no insertion-time or expiry-time ordering captured (CachedTokenValidation stores `expires_at` but it is not consulted in this second pass), so the entries dropped are not the oldest.

Effect: under sustained load once the 10 000-entry cap (Default::new(60, 10000)) is reached, freshly-validated tokens can be evicted while still-live-but-older entries are retained, degrading the SSO introspection cache hit-rate (Epic 104.2) and pushing extra load back onto the PM introspection endpoint — the exact thing the cache exists to avoid. No correctness/security impact (a miss just triggers a real introspection), so severity is low; fix is to sort the eviction candidates by `expires_at` (or use a proper LRU) instead of relying on HashMap order.

backend/servers/reality-server/src/routes/listings.rs:28-34 — clamp_pagination() is documented as the single guard that keeps raw `page`/`limit` query params 'safe before they reach SQL', and it correctly bounds `limit` via `.clamp(1, MAX_LISTINGS_LIMIT)` (100). But `page` is only floored: `page.unwrap_or(1).max(1)` — there is NO upper bound. A public, unauthenticated caller can pass `?page=2000000000` on GET /api/v1/listings.

The unbounded page is then wired into PublicListingQuery (build_listing_query, listings.rs:44-49) and turned into a SQL OFFSET downstream (offset = (page-1)*limit in the api-core repository layer). This is both (a) a deep-pagination resource-exhaustion vector on a public endpoint — a huge OFFSET forces the DB to scan+discard millions of rows per request — and (b) a latent `(page-1)*limit` i32 multiply that can overflow for large page values (panic in debug / wrap in release), the same class of raw-DB/500 failure the function's own doc-comment says it exists to prevent for negative limits.

Fix: clamp `page` to a sane maximum in clamp_pagination (mirroring the limit clamp), or compute a max-page from the total count, so an attacker-supplied page cannot drive an unbounded OFFSET / arithmetic overflow. The clamp function already owns pagination safety for this segment, so the guard belongs here.

backend/servers/reality-server/src/services/saved_search_alerts.rs:225-238 — in the per-search scan loop, once new match ids are found the code enqueues the alert (enqueue_search_alert, lines 217-233) and THEN advances the watermark via `let _ = self.repo.mark_saved_search_matched(&mut *conn, search.id, ids.len() as i64).await` at line 235-238. Fix: propagate/handle the mark_saved_search_matched error after a successful enqueue (e.g. log at error and, ideally, perform enqueue+watermark advance in one transaction so they commit atomically), rather than silently swallowing it and risking duplicate alert delivery.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/push_fanout.rs:367-376 — `send_fcm` (FCM HTTP v1) only flags a device token for eviction when the upstream error status matches `"NOT_REGISTERED" | "UNREGISTERED" | "INVALID_REGISTRATION"`. The second bool of the returned tuple is the 'evict this token' signal (the caller deletes the stored token only when it is true — see the APNs sibling at push_fanout.rs:844-959 which evicts on BadDeviceToken/Unregistered). A token that FCM rejects as INVALID_ARGUMENT is therefore never pruned from storage and is re-attempted on every subsequent fanout, producing a permanent per-fanout failed-send + warn log for that device with no self-healing.

The legacy path `send_fcm_legacy` (push_fanout.rs:449-456) has the same shape: it evicts only on `"NotRegistered" | "InvalidRegistration"` and would likewise retain a token FCM rejects for other permanent reasons.

backend/servers/api-server/src/services/push_fanout.rs:280 — `.expect("reqwest client build should not fail")` and push_fanout.rs:773 — `.expect("reqwest APNs client build should not fail")`. `reqwest::ClientBuilder::build()` is fallible at runtime (it can error on TLS-backend / native-cert-store initialization, not just on programmer misconfiguration), so these are runtime panics living inside the notification-fanout service rather than compile-time invariants.

A panic here aborts the calling task/worker on the push path instead of degrading gracefully (skip-send + error metric). The surrounding code already models graceful degradation for every other failure mode in this file (network errors return `(false, false)`, unconfigured providers early-return with a warn), so panicking on client construction is the odd path out.
Fix: propagate the build error (return a constructor `Result` / mark the provider unconfigured and log) so a TLS/cert init failure disables push fanout instead of crashing the worker.

Systemic across the commonMain repository layer: every repository that wraps a suspend Ktor call in try/catch uses a bare `catch (e: Exception)` and folds the throwable into `Result.failure(e)` WITHOUT first rethrowing kotlinx.coroutines.CancellationException. In Kotlin coroutines, CancellationException is an Exception, so `catch (e: Exception)` swallows it — this breaks structured/cooperative cancellation. Affected files (57 catch sites total): favorites/FavoritesRepository.kt (11), auth/SsoService.kt (9), notifications/NotificationRepository.kt (9), inquiry/InquiryRepository.kt (8), listing/ListingRepository.kt (6), agency/AgencyRepository.kt (4), realtor/PortalListingsRepository.kt (2, lines 62 & 97), realtor/RealtorRepository.kt (2, lines 41 & 61).

The correct pattern already exists in this very codebase: shared/src/commonMain/kotlin/three/two/bit/ppt/reality/layout/LayoutRepository.kt:65-70 does `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` immediately before the generic `catch (e: Exception)`. LayoutRepository is the ONLY of the 10 repos that handles this correctly (grep for CancellationException across commonMain returns only LayoutRepository.kt), which demonstrates the intended convention and that the other 9 repos are inconsistent regressions rather than a deliberate design choice.

Impact: when a composable's rememberCoroutineScope / viewModelScope is cancelled (user navigates away, screen disposed, or a newer request supersedes an in-flight one), the cancelled Ktor call throws CancellationException which is caught and returned as `Result.failure(e)`. Callers then treat a normal cancellation as a real error — e.g. Navigation.kt list loaders do `.onFailure { xxx = emptyList() }`, and screens like AccountScreen surface Log.e / error UI. This produces spurious error states/empty-list flashes on navigation and can interfere with cancellation propagation. Fix: add `catch (e: CancellationException) { throw e }` as the first catch clause in each suspend fun's try/catch (mirroring LayoutRepository), or centralize the request+Result wrapping in a shared helper that rethrows CancellationException. Recommend a follow-up implementer task to sweep the 9 repositories.
